A modern smartphone is an ultra-dense computational system, a fusion of mechanical, electronic, and photonic subsystems operating across scales from centimeters to nanometers, executing upwards of **5 trillion** floating-point operations per second (TFLOPS) while consuming under **10W** of power. The structural integrity of its chassis, composed of **7000-series aluminum**, **titanium alloys**, or **Gorilla Glass Victus 2**, is optimized for impact resistance and thermal dissipation, incorporating microstructured coatings to enhance hydrophobicity and minimize surface adhesion coefficients. Within this enclosure lies the **System-on-Chip (SoC)**, a silicon wafer intricately etched using **Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography (EUV)** at resolutions approaching **3nm**, packing over **20 billion transistors** per **100 mm²**, each operating at switching speeds exceeding **1 ps (picosecond)**.  

The CPU core complex, structured around **ARMv9, x86-64**, or **RISC-V** architectures, consists of **big.LITTLE configurations** where high-performance out-of-order execution cores, clocked at **3.6 GHz**, dynamically hand off tasks to energy-efficient cores at **1.8 GHz**, utilizing **DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling)** controlled by an **AVS (Adaptive Voltage Scaling) regulator**. Multi-threaded workloads are distributed across **8–12 cores**, leveraging **SMT (Simultaneous Multi-Threading)** and **speculative execution**, executing instructions in a **13–15 stage pipeline** with **up to 256-entry reorder buffers**. The integrated **GPU**, often based on **AMD RDNA 3, ARM Mali, or Apple Metal**, incorporates **5,632 ALUs (Arithmetic Logic Units)** across **192 shader cores**, processing **16-bit floating-point operations** at **over 2 TFLOPS**, while supporting **ray tracing acceleration** through **BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy) traversal units**.  

Memory bandwidth is maximized via **LPDDR5X**, operating at **8,500 MT/s**, with a bus width of **128 bits**, yielding effective bandwidths of **136 GB/s**. The NAND flash storage module, based on **UFS 4.0**, integrates **12-plane 3D NAND arrays**, where each die contains **176 layers**, structured as **QLC (Quad-Level Cell) or TLC (Triple-Level Cell)**, achieving sequential read speeds of **4,200 MB/s** and write latencies below **50 μs**. The touchscreen, interfaced through **I²C or SPI protocols**, operates at polling rates exceeding **480 Hz**, resolving touch inputs with spatial accuracy below **0.1 mm**, detecting capacitive differentials on a **20 × 30 microgrid array**, each node measuring impedance at **100 kΩ** thresholds.  

Display technology varies between **AMOLED (Active Matrix Organic Light Emitting Diode)** and **LTPO (Low-Temperature Polycrystalline Oxide) OLED**, featuring **subpixel arrangements** in **RGB PenTile, Stripe, or Delta configurations**, each pixel comprising **3 subpixels** emitting light at **464 THz (red), 540 THz (green), and 620 THz (blue)**. Frame refresh rates range from **1 Hz to 144 Hz**, modulated via **PWM dimming at 2,160 Hz** to reduce perceived flicker. The camera sensor, often a **1/1.3” stacked CMOS BSI (Back-Side Illuminated) sensor**, incorporates **4×4 pixel binning** through **QPDAF (Quad-Pixel Phase Detection Autofocus)**, reading **RAW Bayer data** at **14-bit depth**, processed by an **ISP (Image Signal Processor)** executing **1.2 TOPS (Trillion Operations Per Second)** of computational photography tasks, including **HDR fusion, tone mapping, and Gaussian denoising via bilateral filtering**.  

Wireless communication protocols include **5G NR (New Radio)**, utilizing **sub-6 GHz and mmWave (24 GHz–40 GHz) bands**, achieving peak data rates of **10 Gbps** via **256-QAM (Quadrature Amplitude Modulation)** and **8×8 MIMO (Multiple Input, Multiple Output)**. Wi-Fi connectivity adheres to **802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6E)**, operating within **160 MHz channels** and leveraging **OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access)** for subcarrier multiplexing. Bluetooth **5.3 LE (Low Energy)** transmits at **2 Mbps** per channel, utilizing **AFH (Adaptive Frequency Hopping)** to mitigate interference across the **79 MHz ISM (Industrial, Scientific, and Medical) band**.  

The **Power Management Integrated Circuit (PMIC)** orchestrates energy distribution, dynamically adjusting voltage rails across **13 power domains**, ensuring peak efficiency within a **90%–95% conversion range**. The **Li-Ion battery**, featuring a **graphite anode** and **NMC (Nickel Manganese Cobalt) cathode**, undergoes controlled **CCCV (Constant Current Constant Voltage) charging**, reaching **80% state-of-charge (SoC) within 30 minutes** at **65W** fast charging rates. Battery degradation is monitored via **Coulomb counting** with **ΔV/Δt compensation**, mitigating dendrite formation and thermal runway risks.  

At the quantum level, MOSFET switching dynamics are dictated by **carrier drift velocity saturation at 10⁷ cm/s**, while interconnect resistance in **Copper (Cu) dual-damascene wiring** is constrained by **electron scattering mean free paths of ~39 nm at 300K**. Tunneling leakage, a major challenge in sub-5nm designs, is mitigated through **HKMG (High-K Metal Gate) dielectric stacks**, replacing traditional **SiO₂ (Silicon Dioxide)** with **HfO₂ (Hafnium Dioxide)**, maintaining a dielectric constant of **κ ≈ 25** to suppress gate leakage currents below **1 nA/μm**.  

Executing a simple operation—such as rendering an app transition—triggers a cascade of events, from **UI framework calls** at the **application layer**, through **surface compositing by the GPU**, **VSync synchronization**, **framebuffer swaps**, and **pixel voltage modulations at the OLED panel**, all occurring within a **16.67 ms (60 Hz) window**, ensuring perceptual fluidity. Meanwhile, background processes such as **garbage collection in the ART (Android Runtime)** or **instruction retirement in speculative execution pipelines** continue in parallel, maintaining system efficiency under peak workloads exceeding **100 GOPS (Giga Operations Per Second)**.  

Every interaction with the device is an emergent consequence of **billions of transistor state changes**, governed by the principles of **quantum mechanics, semiconductor physics, and electromagnetic wave propagation**, woven together in a computational fabric executing at near-light-speed limits, constrained only by thermodynamic dissipation, quantum tunneling barriers, and the relentless march toward ever-decreasing process nodes.

text: Suggestion:  before backing up/uploading to GPhotos, organize them into folder/s on your PC by event, or subject, or item.  Windows has excellent Batch Processing functionality.  Once in File Explorer, locate your folder.  Be sure to click "View" tab where you will then see "Panes" and also "Layout" sections at top.  Both should be set to "Details."  Then rename the folder to whatever: "1970 Jones Family Vacation" or "Jones 1970 Family Vacation."  Then highlight all the related photos within it (do NOT include videos).  Right click & rename one, using same name as folder. They will all be named the same with a sequential (#) following.  Then, while all are highlighted, edit the detailed metadata shown in the far right column with whatever...Date Taken, Location, Comments, Title, Tags, etc.  After batch processing your event photos, THEN upload to Google Photos and the basic, important metadata, including date, will stay with each photo, and sort by date.

text: I know one way to get around this issue, but in involves an extra step taking more time. When you select photos for an album, you can also choose to archive these same photos. Then they will still show up in your album that you created & they will also now show up in your archive section, but they will no longer show up in your main photos category. This will allow you to keep track of your progress if you are wanting to sort through all of your photos, putting them each in different albums. You archive every photo that you put in an album. Your remaining photos that are left to be sorted will keep getting smaller until there is none left. Once you finish sorting everything, you could choose to move them all back out of archive & your main photos section would return to normal, or you could choose to leave them in archive & your photos section would be empty, but it would be replaced by your archive section. I would probably choose to leave them in archive to make any future sorting easier. The downside to all of this is that it takes up twice the amount of time. You spend time moving some pictures to a new album. Then immediately after, you take an additional step moving those same pictures to archive. I'm not aware of any way to move pictures to both an album & archive in one step. So this plan sucks, but it should work. Google needs to create a better way to do this.

text:
Hi there, thank you for your question.  If you didn't save a photo to your Photos app or another designated location, it may still be possible to retrieve it, depending on the source of the photo and the device you're using. Here are a few methods to try:

1. Check the original source: Go back to the original source where you found the photo, such as a website, email attachment, or messaging app. You may be able to download or save the photo again.

2. Check the app's cache or temporary storage: Some apps, like web browsers and messaging apps, temporarily store images in a cache or temporary folder. You can try looking for the image in these folders, but accessing these folders may require technical expertise or third-party apps.

3. Check your device's Downloads folder: If you downloaded the photo, it might be saved in your device's Downloads folder by default. Open the Files app (Android) or Finder (macOS) and navigate to the Downloads folder to check for the photo.

4. Check the Recently Deleted album (iOS and macOS): If you're using an iPhone, iPad, or Mac, check the Recently Deleted album in the Photos app. Photos deleted from the Photos app are stored in this album for 30 days before being permanently removed.

text: I could be wrong, but here's what may be happening to you because it happened to me. I was using the native Gallery app on my Android phone to organize/move my photos into certain albums (which are really just device folders). When I would then open the Google Photos app on my phone, I'd see those groups of folders with the same titles I had given them in the Gallery app. But those are not ALBUMS in the Google Photos app. I then needed to create Albums, but I didn't know this for a while, though. So when I would delete a folder (album) from the phone's Gallery app, I would notice that same-titled folder was now gone from the Photos app. I KNEW I had backed up all my photos but didn't understand where the folder went. Turns out, the photos were still in my Google Photos app, but just in chronological order. When I deleted the device folder "album" from my phone, it also deleted the folder from the Google Photos app but not the photos inside. They were still there, just in chronological order. So, what I should've been doing all along, was using the Google Photos app to create albums and organize my photos. The part that had confused me all along is that my phone's Gallery app calls the folders with the photos "albums" but they are really device folders. Creating an album in the Gallery app does not create an Album in Photos.

text:
Anyone who has access to your phone will also have access to your google photos And to your Locked folder inside Google photos. 

The only thing this app does is to upload the photos to the cloud server under your Google account and it uses the same biometrics/password/pin set up for your phone in order to access the account.

What this app hides is your photos from other non-google apps. Google itself can view each and every photo backed up to its servers without need to access your phone directly.

In short, if you have any photos you want hidden then DO NOT USE OR INSTALL GOOGLE PHOTOS!!! Once installed it will automatically scan and back up to its servers every photo you have. 

If you want to keep anything private, use the android hidden folder instead, but be aware that 1. this uses up main memory and cannot be moved to an SD card, and 2. as soon as photos are removed from the hidden folder (such as to offload to a computer), Google photos will detect it and immediately upload to the cloud if it is still installed.

text:
Moving a photo to an external location to which Google photos does not have access and then deleting the photo from Google photos will, of course, not delete the photo from your other location. It will, however, delete the photo from your phone since the app has access to your phone.

That said, under Utilities there is a Free Up Space option that will remove all photos on your phone that are already backed up on the Google servers. There is also a Delete From Device option for each photo that will do this for each individual photo. 

There is a way of removing photos from the Google photos server while keeping them on the phone and not using an external location. If you move the photos on the device to the Android Secure Folder then Google will not have access to the file on the phone when it is deleted from their server. Look into how to set that up if you want to "protect" your photos from Google deletion.
